Minor sags can be monitored or kept clear with cleaning. Significant sags and collapsed sections are repaired by excavating and relaying that section at the correct fall. A camera inspection measures how bad it is.</p></div><figure class="artlead"><img src="/uploads/is-it-possible-to-repair-a-sagging-sewer-line.jpg" width="800" height="800" alt="Camera footage of water pooling in a sagging section of sewer pipe" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async" sizes="(max-width:1024px) 100vw, 610px"></figure><h2 id="s-what">What a sag or belly is</h2><p>Sewer pipe is laid with a steady fall so waste runs downhill to the main. If part of the line settles, that section dips below the pipe either side. Water collects in the dip, solids settle, and paper and grease build up until the line blocks. On camera it looks like the pipe filling with water partway along, then emptying again beyond the low point.</p><h2 id="s-causes">What causes a sewer line to sag or collapse</h2><ul class="dots"><li>Poor bedding or compaction when the pipe was laid</li><li>Soil movement, especially reactive clay that swells and shrinks</li><li>Sandy soil washing away around a leaking joint</li><li>Heavy loads from vehicles over a shallow pipe</li><li>Tree roots pushing pipe sections out of line</li><li>Nearby excavation disturbing the ground</li></ul><aside class="artmid" data-label="Urgency">Repair needed</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="tnote">Guide only. The camera measures the sag depth and length.</p><h2 id="s-repair">Can a sagging sewer line be repaired?</h2><p>Yes. The right repair depends on severity. A shallow sag that holds a little water may only need monitoring and occasional cleaning. A deep sag that holds waste, or any collapsed section, is repaired by excavating that section and relaying the pipe on proper bedding at the right grade.</p><p>Relining is not a reliable fix for a significant sag, because the liner follows the dip. It is often used on the rest of the line once the sagging section has been replaced, which keeps excavation to the minimum. See <a href="/pipe-relining-vs-replacement-sydney/">pipe relining vs replacement</a>.</p><h2 id="s-cost">What affects the cost of repair</h2><p>Depth of the pipe, length of the failed section, what sits above it (lawn, paving, concrete or a structure) and access for excavation all affect the price. The camera footage and locator position are what allow an accurate quote rather than an estimate.</p><h2 id="s-faq">Frequently asked questions</h2><div class="faqs"><details class="faq"><summary><span class="fq-mark"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-chev-down"></use></svg></span>How do I know if my sewer line is sagging?</summary><div class="fq-body"><p>A drain that slows or blocks again soon after clearing, repeated blockages at the same point, and water pooling partway along the pipe on camera are the usual signs. A CCTV inspection confirms the sag and measures its depth and length.</p></div></details><details class="faq"><summary><span class="fq-mark"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-chev-down"></use></svg></span>Can a sagging sewer line be fixed without digging?</summary><div class="fq-body"><p>Usually not for a significant sag, because a liner follows the dip. Minor sags may be managed with cleaning. Severe sags and collapses are excavated and relaid, often with relining used on the rest of the line.</p></div></details><details class="faq"><summary><span class="fq-mark"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-chev-down"></use></svg></span>Is a sagging sewer pipe an emergency?</summary><div class="fq-body"><p>Not always. A minor sag can be monitored. It becomes urgent if the line blocks repeatedly, sewage overflows, or the ground above is sinking, which suggests the pipe is broken.</p></div></details><details class="faq"><summary><span class="fq-mark"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-chev-down"></use></svg></span>What causes a sewer pipe to collapse?</summary><div class="fq-body"><p>Old brittle pipe, soil movement, heavy loads above a shallow pipe, tree roots and nearby excavation are the usual causes. A sag often comes before a collapse.</p></div></details><details class="faq"><summary><span class="fq-mark"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-chev-down"></use></svg></span>Who pays to repair a sagging sewer line?</summary><div class="fq-body"><p>The property owner is responsible for the private sewer up to the connection with the Sydney Water main. If the fault is in the main, Sydney Water handles it. See <a href="/who-is-responsible-for-a-blocked-sewer-sydney/">who is responsible for a blocked sewer</a>.</p></div></details><details class="faq"><summary><span class="fq-mark"><svg class="ico" aria-hidden="true"><use href="#i-chev-down"></use></svg></span>Will insurance cover a collapsed sewer?</summary><div class="fq-body"><p>Some policies cover sudden damage and its consequences, but gradual deterioration and root damage are often excluded. Check your policy and keep the camera footage for any claim.</p></div></details></div><h2 id="s-next">What to do next</h2><p>If you suspect a sag or collapse, book a <a href="/services/cctv-drain-inspection/">CCTV drain inspection</a>.
